Near-death experiences are often related to the same things that happen while hallucinating on drugs. Effectively, its a breakdown in communication between various parts of the brain. As we die, signals crossing through various parts of the brain begin to sort of "descynchronize", and our brains replace missing information with its "best guess". It is suspected that is why people's lives "flash" before their eyes...the brain is replacing missing or damaged information with information it already has, in the form of memories. In many ways, this is similar to the effects achieved by hallucinogens, anesthetics, or even something as simple as the Ganzfeld Effect.

As for the idea of an afterlife, this was likely an invention of society coupled with natural fear responses. It is biologically favorable to fear things you are unfamiliar with or do not understand, as in the wild, these things can be dangerous or deadly. Thus, a healthy fear of the unknown becomes a favorably selected trait. In civilized society (even something as basic as "caveman" society), certain behaviors are favorable for the group. For example, members of the group not killing other members of the same group is typically favorable for the group as a whole. So, behavioral codes become established (or, later, legal codes) which govern the group. It is likely that the idea of an afterlife, gods, deities, etc. formed both as a way of helping to explain the unknown while in turn reinforcing the the behavioral codes of conduct that made societies more successful.

All of that said, I am an engineer in nuclear waste, not an anthropologist or biologist. So, take everything above with a generous helping of salt.

Perhaps the common ancestor that developed near-death hallucinations also developed something that increased chances of survival. The ancestor mated, and passed on both mutations.

The concept of "after-life" is obviously not itself evolutionary, but cultural. The effects of near-death experiences are very similar to those of hallucinogens as @NuclearTrashMan pointed out. An ancestral human individual with no concept of "after-life" experiencing these phenomena would not necessarily assume it was a glimpse into the here-after any more than he would think that after eating the wrong kind of mushrooms in the wild; he may, however, interpret whatever activity lead him to that experience as unfavorable to his survival and seek to avoid it in the future, where possible. This would be beneficial from an evolutionary standpoint, and could easily be selected for.

Regarding the religious/spiritual concept of after-life, an interesting analysis if its invention can be found in terror management theory, specifically regarding mortality salience. Basically, the theory is that humans, with our relatively unique cognitive ability to foresee our own inevitable deaths even in the absence of immediate threats, developed cultural, rather than innately psychological, mechanisms to manage the anxiety generated by contemplation of our mortality. Like any theory it has its flaws, but is generally interesting to ponder.
